The word “is” can mean that something exists in itself, or only that it is affirmed in relation to something else. The second sense is enough for the point here. — س ره

This kind of affirmation is part of how we explain a negation; it is not something that exists within the negation, as some commentators on Aristotle have claimed. What is denied cannot exist together with its denial. When we say that sight is part of the definition of blindness, we do not mean that sight exists in the blind person. We mean that blindness can be explained only by referring to sight. A definition may contain more than the thing defined. — س ره

For possibility to apply to something, it must do so necessarily; otherwise, it could change. Thus the possibility of a thing must be necessary in the mind, the mind's recognition of that necessity must also be necessary, and the sequence would continue without end. — س ره

The underlying essence remains the same, though it can exist in different ways. At one time it may exist only as a dependent relation; at another, as something the mind can consider in its own right. Think of matter taking on a form and then exchanging it for another. Matter remains through the change, but matter together with its first form does not itself turn into matter together with the second. The author's comparison and the commentator's comparison differ slightly: the author compares dependent existence to matter, while the commentator compares it to a form that can leave matter. The point is that the essence or meaning remains through both modes of existence, like matter remains through successive forms. In the example of the concepts “relation” and “independent thing,” the shared idea that remains is the meaning common to both the relational use and the independent use. — س ره

This example is not sound: two opposite qualities cannot belong to one and the same existence. The two parts would differ in existence, especially for anyone who thinks that different qualities produce an actual division in the thing that bears them. A better example, on the philosopher's account, would be that every part of a continuous body can itself be divided into further parts. — س ره
Finitude is a negative feature that necessarily belongs to whatever is finite. — س ره

This refutes the claim that necessary connections exist in reality through the things from which they are drawn, as is often said about abstract concepts. If this were so, there would be no difference between a defining feature and an incidental one. I would say that the difference remains: the source exists in itself, while its role as what makes the connection fit to be drawn is incidental. In reality, that readiness or capacity in the source is what the incidental connection consists in. — س ره
These objections are mistaken and do not land. — ط

The answer is first by counterexample: we can truthfully say of every part of a single continuous body that it is a substance and can be divided, even when no actual division has taken place. Second, the parts themselves exist in the world through the existence of the whole, even if their being separate parts does not yet exist. The whole exists even though the description “whole” is relative to its parts. Treating the part's being a part as though it were its own underlying existence is a mistake. The subject of the external judgment may be the parts without an actual division; an imagined division is enough, especially since the parts in thought reflect the parts in the thing. Matter is what can be divided; the divided parts are parts of the matter, not forms imposed on it. The existence of matter can support a true external judgment about those parts because the subject of the judgment is considered in the appropriate way. — س ره

I say that the careful philosopher does not base a true judgment about the world on a relation that exists only as a possibility before the mind draws it out. Rather, the judgment rests on the actual existence of the thing from which that relation can be drawn. That source exists in the world, and the relation is drawn from its readiness to support the judgment. If you say that the source exists in itself, not the relation, then this does not answer the original objection. The source's existence is not the same as the existence of the incidental relation. The commentator compares this with the philosophers' distinction between general and detailed knowledge: the relevant knowledge exists in one unified way even when it is not present as a separate idea of each thing. So these necessary connections may not exist as distinct forms, but they exist together in one reality that is their source. — س ره
There is a third kind: existence that is actually present in a general, undivided way. It is neither existence in every separate detail nor mere potential existence. — س ره

These are actual judgments, so they require their subjects to exist even more than possible judgments do. The reply is that, for this philosopher, their subjects exist through the source from which their existence is drawn. They do not exist as independent things, but they do have an actual, dependent existence. This is why the judgment is stronger than a merely possible one. — س ره

On the contrary, it means exactly that we can say of Zayd, before he exists, that he may become a writer. The author objects that writing is a condition in the world and such a condition needs a subject that exists there. If he means actual writing, I grant that it is a condition in the world. But we are not saying Zayd is actually writing. We are saying only that he could write, which remains true even if he never comes to exist. If he means that the possibility of writing is an external condition, ordinary possibility is a denial, not an existing quality. Readiness to write is different: that is a feature we can attribute to a subject, not a qualification of a statement, which is our subject here.

His own admission that possibility, considered simply as the link in a statement, does not demand an existing subject supports the philosopher he is criticizing. It is possible that the author means to rely on an argument he will give later in the second stage, in the chapter following the discussion of restoring what has ceased to exist. There he maintains that negative as well as affirmative statements require a subject, even though denial considered simply as denial does not. The familiar rule that negations apply more broadly concerns how we consider them. Likewise, possibility considered on its own does not require an existing subject, whereas a statement that something is possible may do so. Keep this distinction in mind. — س ره

General possibility means either that the subject's own existence is not impossible, in a simple statement, or that the relation between subject and predicate is not impossible, in a compound statement. For God, whose existence is identical with His reality, it means that His own existence is not impossible. For possible things, whose existence differs from their essence, it means that the relation of existence to their essence is not impossible. It can also mean that no possible mode of existence is impossible for the divine reality, since every such mode is only an illuminating relation to Him. — س ره

The opposite side should be understood as the opposite itself, so the description applies to the subject, not merely to something related to it. This is sound only if the opposite is taken as a sign pointing to the subject, rather than as the subject itself. — ط

Possibility properly describes the opposing side, since it means that necessity is denied. So when it is applied to the other side of the statement, the description is figurative: the side is described through what it is connected to. — س ره

Sharing a meaning requires only a common concept, such as “thing.” It does not require an unfinished broader kind that is made complete by both the Necessary and the possible. That would make God composite from a broader kind and a distinguishing feature. — س ره

Someone may object that strict possibility and impossibility are not real “materials” or components, since both are negative. The answer is that “real” here includes whatever holds in the facts, whether through existence or nonexistence. But general possibility is not a component of a thing because it is merely a denial of the necessity of the opposite. Strict possibility, by contrast, has its own distinct use, and generality belongs to its meaning. It is like saying that “animal, considered as a universal” exists in the world: the added condition of universality is only in the mind. — س ره

The explanation is not perfectly precise, because it makes strict possibility sound like a compound of two negative features, each applied figuratively. Yet the essence really is possible, and possibility is one meaning, not a combination of two. — ط

Animality, for example, is possible because neither its existence nor its nonexistence is necessary. The same is true of moving one’s fingers and of an eclipse. Yet each is tied to a necessity arising from its subject: from what the subject is, from a description of it, or from a particular time. Examples include being human, being a writer, or the time when an eclipse occurs. These conditions bring necessity with them, so such cases are not possible in all three senses of predication. Writing for a human being is different: it is possible in itself and possible given human nature. Still, writing is necessary once it exists, which is why future possibility is also considered. — س ره

An objection may be raised: writing is not necessary for human nature in general, yet it is necessary when a person is writing. Since nothing exists unless it is necessary, writing conditioned on its actual presence must be necessary. The answer is that this necessity and possibility can apply to the same case from different points of view. Writing is necessary insofar as it exists, but possible insofar as we consider its nature. Its existence is necessary; its essence is possible. — س ره

Tusi explains why the earlier philosopher says this meaning “seems narrower” than the other two, rather than simply calling it narrower. A general term and a specific term share one meaning, with the specific term applying to fewer cases. “Animal” applies to human beings because the meaning of animal is included in the meaning of human being. But “possibility” is used here for different meanings by the same word, not because one meaning contains the other. It is like calling one Black person “the Black”: the word applies to that person and to a wider group in different senses, not as a general term and a specific one. Another commentator develops the same point: even if the meanings of possibility were entirely separate, the word could still be used for both. So this is only a kind of figurative narrowing, not a true case of one meaning being a subset of another. — س ره

Each new meaning comes closer than the one before it to the true midpoint. In the earlier sense, a predicate conditioned on its subject was already necessary. A future event has not yet occurred, so it remains genuinely possible. — س ره
Future events are usually possible, though not always. Sunrise, for example, is necessary. — س ره
This is what the great Tusi establishes in his commentary on the logic of The Remarks and Admonitions. — س ره
That is, the causes and conditions that must be in place for a thing to come into being. — ه ره

Someone might object: if every denial is true of an essence at its own level, then possibility must be true of it there, since possibility includes the denial that existence and nonexistence are necessary. The answer is that this is true, but the denial of that denial is true as well. Just as possibility is not identical with the essence or a part of it, the denial of possibility is neither identical with nor a part of the essence. — س ره

The wording seems mistaken, because possibility is itself a denial, and the text says that these denials are expressed in negative statements. Here, the other denials may have been mentioned only in passing. Changing “first” to “second” in the text would not fix the problem, since necessity and impossibility are not negative statements. The wording would make sense if read as “their opposites”: the denials of necessary existence and necessary nonexistence, which together define possibility. I suspect the original instead said “its two parts”—the denial of the necessity of existence and the denial of the necessity of nonexistence—with “first” and “second” reversed. — س ره

This explains the exception for possible essences considered in themselves. If the division says that a thing, in reality, is never outside the three categories, then it is exhaustive. But if it says the same of a thing at every level, including its own essence considered just as it is, that is false: at that level, the essence may be none of the three. Even if one category were said to belong to it there, the division would still not be exhaustive. Possibility cannot be identical with the essence, since possibility is a denial while the essence has its own distinct content. Nor can it be a part of the essence, since then the essence would be itself plus possibility. The essence cannot be necessary or impossible; if it is possible, possibility itself would have to be possible, and the same question would arise again without end. — س ره

This means the source of necessity. Necessity as a way of relating a predicate to a subject cannot exist at the level of God’s essence; what exists there is its source, the fullness of existence. It is like saying that relational attributes are additional to the divine essence, while what grounds them is the essence itself. — س ره

A reader might ask: if possibility is not in an essence at its own level, why do philosophers call it essential? Because there are two different claims. Possibility may be true of an essence without being identical with it or forming part of it. The philosophers who call it essential mean that it follows from the essence itself; this is “essential” in the sense used in the Book of Demonstration. The present argument denies only that possibility is a piece of the essence, in the sense used in the Isagoge. In other words, something can be said of an essence because of what it is, without being part of its definition. The commentator also distinguishes what possibility is said of from what directly grounds that claim: if possibility comes from the essence itself, the essence is its ground; if it comes from something added, the essence is only what the claim is about. — س ره

Here existence is the predicate in a simple statement such as “God exists.” That first kind concerns necessary existence itself; those that follow concern necessary relations between a subject and what is said of it. In a simple statement of existence, we are not saying that one thing belongs to another. Existence is not a link between them. The first necessity therefore belongs to existence itself; the others concern what must hold in a relationship. Another difference is that the author calls necessity “eternal” in the first case and “essential” in the others. You may ask: if a simple statement of existence contains no such relationship, especially when it concerns God, how can necessity describe the character of a relationship? I reply: at this stage we are only setting out the alternatives; the proof has yet to be examined. — س ره

Or two contradictories, or two similar things, combined in a way that makes the whole impossible. Neither of two opposites need be impossible by itself; what is impossible is putting them together in this way. You may object: if a combination, considered simply as a combination, is possible, what is impossible here? I reply: as a combination it is possible, but as a combination of these particular things it is impossible. Something impossible in what it means may still be formed as an object of thought. — س ره
The discussion relevant here has already appeared. Keep it in mind. — س ره

A possible thing can be considered in two ways. First, we can consider its essence as an existing thing whose existence is separate from other things. When we relate it to God, all the other factors that contribute to its existence—intermediaries, causes, conditions, and what prepares it—join with God to make up its complete cause. Second, we can consider its existence as linked to other things, so that it cannot exist unless they do. “Zayd,” for example, may mean the person born to ʿAmr and Fāṭima at a certain time and place, and so on. On this view, his existence is linked to the whole network of causes and conditions, and bringing him into existence means bringing that whole network into being. In this sense, God is his complete cause. Most philosophical discussions use the first way of considering a possible thing. It follows that a possible thing is necessary relative to another only when considered in relation to its complete cause, or to something that shares that complete cause. Otherwise it remains only possible relative to that other thing. A Necessary Being, by contrast, can only be necessary relative to a possible thing, since the possible thing’s existence depends on it. — ط

Examples are a human being’s speech and a donkey’s braying. This is true when we consider their nearby causes. If we trace those causes back to the Cause of causes, they are necessary relative to it. — س ره

One example is the impossibility of a vacuum considered alongside the absence of whiteness from something that can be white. Here, “because of” should be understood as “in the case of,” as in the Qur'anic phrase “establish prayer at the sun’s decline.” This avoids an objection based on the absence of the First Effect, which is possible in itself, and the absence of God, which is impossible in itself: the relation between these absences is necessity, not possibility. The rule can also be extended to essentially possible things and what follows from their essences, since there is no relation between them and a creator in whether they are brought into being. The answer will be that whatever entails something impossible in itself is itself impossible in itself. On this reading, “because of” means “on account of,” not “at the time of.” — س ره
An effect has no independent existence of its own; its existence is entirely dependent on its cause. — س ره
That is, the absence of the cause considered in relation to the effect’s existence, and the cause’s existence considered in relation to the effect’s absence. — س ره

Someone may object that this does not answer the question about a thing changing from one state to another, since possibility as “lack of necessity” is still part of the objection. The answer is that a thing possible in itself does not demand either side, so it does not conflict with something else requiring it to exist. It is like any subject ready to receive a feature. But a thing necessary in itself does require existence, so another thing could not make it possible: removing its necessity would also remove the existence its nature requires. Similarly, if possibility meant a demand for nonexistence, and something else supplied existence, the two demands would conflict. — س ره

There are three relevant kinds of statement. In a simple negative statement, such as “Zayd is not a writer,” we consider the subject and predicate, then deny that they are connected. In an affirmative statement with a negative predicate, such as “Zayd is a non-writer,” we affirm that a negative feature belongs to the subject. A statement with a negative subject and a negative predicate has both kinds of negation. The first statement has four parts in the mind: the subject, the predicate, their possible connection, and the denial of that connection. The affirmative statement with a negative predicate adds a fifth: assigning the negative feature to the subject. In a statement with a negative subject and predicate, both terms are themselves treated as statements. This is why “Zayd is not a writer” differs from “Zayd is a non-writer”: in the first, the denial comes before the connecting verb; in the second, the connection is affirmed and the predicate is negative. The second kind of statement still requires the subject to exist, because it assigns something to that subject. Some logicians deny this and say that “vacuum is nonexistent” does not require a vacuum to exist as its subject. But the proper way to say that no vacuum exists is “No vacuum is existent,” which does not assume a vacuum as a subject. Then the broader claim “Nothing existent is perceptible” would be false. The same issue appears in an argument that says, “A substance is not an accident; whatever is not an accident does not need a subject.” The first statement is affirmative with a negative predicate, not a simple denial. — س ره

Three objections are raised. First, if possibility is only a denial, and denial removes the connection between subject and predicate, possibility could not be a way of qualifying a statement alongside necessity and impossibility. Second, if possibility is two denials taken together, it would not be one simple meaning like necessity and impossibility. Third, this would contradict the earlier claim that possibility is the positive statement that both necessities are absent. The answer is to distinguish the essence considered just as it is from the mind’s judgment about it. Of an essence in itself, we make two simple denials: its existence is not necessary, and its nonexistence is not necessary. These denials contain no further judgment. The mind can then restate them as one affirmative claim: the essence is such that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary. That is how possibility is affirmed of the essence. Since this affirmative claim is true of the essence, it requires a basis; and because nothing else is under consideration, its basis is the essence itself. This avoids all three objections. It also resolves the apparent conflict between an essence’s own lack of necessity and the necessity or impossibility it receives through another. The first claim concerns the essence by itself, where there is no demand either way. The second concerns the essence together with its cause. The statements differ in meaning and refer to different circumstances, so they do not conflict. — ط

The equal relation between existence and nonexistence follows from the meaning of possibility. The positive statement that an essence is possible is true when the essence exists, either in the world or in the mind. Someone might object that if the essence itself requires both sides to remain equal, the earlier problem still stands, even if that requirement is not the meaning of possibility. The answer is that this requirement is only a requirement not to require either side. — س ره

The discussion is about how possibility is predicated of an essence, not the first, mental grasp of what possibility means. The claim that it is true to say that neither necessity applies is mentioned in another work, The Clear Horizon, but there too it is not presented as the meaning of possibility, only as something that follows from it. “Being true” is itself a concept. Here, a simple denial means a bare refusal of a connection, which does not require the subject to exist. A negative predicate, by contrast, describes the absence of a feature in a subject and therefore does require a subject to exist. Some writers call this an affirmative statement with a negative predicate. In that sense, the positive statement discussed above resembles it. — س ره

This argument is included among the kinds of possibility because someone might object: if possibility is neither the essence nor part of it, then it must be an incidental feature that needs a cause; and if it is caused by something else, possibility would be “through another.” The answer is that, as the author explains, the possible thing has only bare potentiality. Possibility is not something made, and the essence is not a maker. The terminology therefore does not force the conclusion. Also, a feature that needs a cause is one added to a subject; not every feature that can be said of a subject is an added feature of that kind. — س ره

This applies to the cause of existence as well, though this existence is like nonexistence because it is pure potentiality: the existence of prime matter. Prime matter is also a co-cause, since a form helps bring matter into existence. The form in question is one separate being. — س ره

This is the view of the distinguished philosopher Dāmād: in judgments, nonexistence follows the pattern of existence, unity, and plurality. Just as the identity of an effect’s nonexistence follows the identity of that effect’s existence, the nonexistence of a particular complete cause follows the identity of that cause. The many absences are absences of separate parts and conditions, not multiple instances of the absence of the complete cause—just as the parts of a whole may exist separately without dividing the real whole into separate wholes. — س ره

It is contradictory to say that a thing’s possibility in general comes from something else while, by itself, it could still be possible, necessary, or impossible. If its possibility comes from another, how can it have any of these statuses in itself? Also, “allowed” here means “conceivable,” not possibility in itself. — س ره

This is disputed. If we suppose the other has no effect, the thing may still be possible in itself, as the first argument says. The two arguments are called groundless for the reason just given, not because they take possibility to mean that the essence itself demands the outcome. The commentator adds that they may be further objections to an earlier proposal, and that some of their problems are too obvious to need stating. — س ره

The denial applies to the qualifier. So to say “a human being, considered in itself, is neither existent nor nonexistent” means that existence is not the human being’s own special nature, either identical with it or a part of it. This does not mean that the human being lacks existence altogether, since existence can belong to it in another way. — س ره

This distinction does not hold in every case. Sometimes a thing is rightly said to lack both a feature and its opposite when considered in itself, as with features that belong to an essence only on condition that it exists, such as writing or motion. In other cases, when a feature belongs to an essence without that condition, the essence is not free of one side or the other, even when considered in itself. Existence, unity, possibility, and thinghood are examples. So an essence considered in itself is free of features that arise only with existence and of their opposites, but its own essential features are different: the essence is not the source of them, even when one side cannot be denied of it. The rule about where the denial belongs applies to the essence’s own features. If we say “a human being, considered in itself, is not existent,” the denial is about existence in any form, which would wrongly make the essence entirely without existence. That is not the same as denying a feature that can be absent at the essence’s own level, as explained earlier. — س ره

The best answer may be that possibility is a simple denial, expressed by “is not” in the incomplete sense, and this kind of denial cannot itself be denied by another simple denial. The denial that is denied in the phrase “the denial of the denial of both necessities” is instead a negative feature used as a predicate. Denying that feature does not remove possibility. — ط
This is part of the opposing speaker’s argument, which makes its weakness even clearer. — س ره

The author seems to be responding to an earlier objection: if possibility is only a denial, it cannot be a way of qualifying a statement alongside necessity and impossibility, since a denial removes the connection between subject and predicate, while a qualification describes that connection. He replies that possibility, though negative, is a positive state of the subject; therefore, the statement is affirmative with a negative predicate. But earlier he said that the division into the three categories is really two divisions: first, between what must exist and what need not; then, among what need not exist, between what must not exist and what is neither necessary nor impossible. In that second division, the negative is already being used as a predicate. The author’s claim that a simple negative statement merely removes a connection, rather than affirming a negative connection, also makes it hard to explain how a negative feature can be positively assigned. — ط

This seems to conflict with what was said earlier: possibility is the essence’s lack of demand for either necessity, not its demand that both necessities be denied. Perhaps the earlier passage explained possibility in itself, while this passage explains what it means to say, in a division, that an essence that exists in the world or in thought is possible. The statement is affirmative with a negative predicate, even if possibility itself is a simple denial. When a subject exists, it can be described as having that denial. In this sense, being described as possible, though it belongs to a level prior to existence, works like being described as existent. — س ره

Another answer is that possibility is the denial of both necessities from all eternity. The familiar distinction is between “the possibility of the world’s eternity,” which is false, and “the eternity of its possibility,” which is true. The denial in the objection is a denial that begins at some point, not an eternal one. If possibility came from another, it would not be eternal. — س ره

The same objection also applies to the author. Earlier he said that dividing an essence into the necessary, the impossible, and the possible amounts to two divisions, each built from a thing and its opposite. On that account, the two denials are separate in thought and cannot be one unless they are considered in another way, such as as an affirmative statement with a negative predicate. This also shows the weakness of the earlier attempt to make possibility such a statement. Neither answer fully resolves the objection. If the claim “the essence is possible through another” is true, it is an ordinary claim about the essence, not part of its definition. But the argument would then imply that the essence exists without a cause of its existence or a cause of its nonexistence. That is impossible in reality, because it would make the essence neither existent nor nonexistent—not merely “neither” when considered at the level of its own essence. — ط

This does not answer the objection. The absence of necessity still needs a cause; if the essence is not its cause, something else must be. That would leave two absences caused by something else, which is precisely possibility through another. — ط

“Added in the world” describes these things; it does not mean that what is added is an object beyond the thing it describes. The following words—“but they are added in the mind”—make this clear. — س ره

The author earlier tried to reconcile the positions by saying that these concepts have dependent existence, not existence in themselves. This works for the three categories, but not for existence and unity—unless “existence” here means the act of affirming that something exists, or the verbal concept “to exist.” — س ره
This argument assumes Suhrawardi’s view that every whole made of parts exists as one distinct thing in its own right. — س ره

The example is light. For him, light has the same underlying reality whether it exists on its own or as a feature of something else. Later, in the discussion of God, he explains that knowledge, power, will, and similar things may be qualities at one level, independent realities at another, and necessary in themselves at the highest. — س ره

You might object that being caused is different from being known. But whatever makes it true to say that a thing is caused—whether that basis is real or something recognised by the mind—must also make it true to say that God knows it. Otherwise something would escape His knowledge, which embraces all things. This is even clearer for simple realities, from which things made of parts ultimately arise. — س ره

If “the disputing group” means the followers of the First Teacher who accept the reality of possibility, the point is clear. If it means theologians, as the wording suggests, the argument is a proof, not a debate framed in their own accepted premises. It uses assumptions they would not accept, such as the existence of an intellect and the claim that the First Effect is eternal and created directly. It also assumes that coming into being means having been preceded by nonexistence in one’s own being, whereas they say it means being preceded by another; and that possibility is what makes a thing need a cause. It also assumes that one source can produce many things only if it acts in different ways. — س ره

Someone might ask: could the Necessary Being produce possibility first and the First Effect afterwards, so that He would not be producing two things at once? No. Possibility cannot exist on its own, and a feature cannot cause the very thing to which it belongs. Besides, this would mean that the First Effect was not really first. — س ره

This dependence is what is meant by causation; other kinds of dependence mean only that two things cannot be separated. A feature belongs to an essence in itself because it belongs to it when considered just as it is, without regard to whether it exists in the world or in the mind. It would belong to the essence even if the essence could be considered apart from both kinds of existence. But an essence considered apart from its relation to a creator is, by agreement, only an idea. What belongs to it in that way is all the more clearly only an idea. — س ره
One of the two descriptions is a mental state—the lack of necessity—while the other is an actual state. There is no contradiction between an actual existence and a mental nonexistence. — س ره
The description belongs to existence and nonexistence. Some copies use a feminine dual form, but that reading is incorrect. — س ره
That is, for the description to apply to things in the world, it would need dependent existence there, as explained several times above. — س ره

This applies even to impossibility. The impossibility of being made of stone applies to a human being as a dependent description in the world. But the impossibility of a partner to God or of opposites being joined is only assumed in thought, since these subjects do not exist as definite things. — س ره

To describe something as having a feature in the world, the thing must exist there; the feature need not exist there as a separate thing. The same applies when we say that something is true of a subject. We must also distinguish the ideas discussed in general philosophy from the ideas studied in logic: they do not describe things in exactly the same way. — س ره

The same applies to individuality. It means that the very idea cannot be thought of as true of many things; but thought is a second-order concept. A natural individual—the thing to which individuality applies in the world—is not a logical or mental individual. If “individual” means a thing made distinct, which is existence itself, then it is more fully real in the world than anything else. — س ره

One could say this follows from the author’s view that logic is part of philosophy and that the subjects studied by logic have some kind of reality outside the mind. He will return to this later. — س ره

One possibility cannot differ from another simply by being possible: possibility has one meaning. Nor can matter make them different, since matter, considered in itself, has no distinctions. And the future things to which they refer cannot distinguish them either, since those things do not yet exist. If each possibility is said to differ only because it is a different possibility, the argument goes in a circle.

This argument also seems to apply to readiness in matter, even though that readiness exists in the world; so the proof would wrongly make it only mental. It also applies to any number of possibilities, not only an unlimited number. The answer to the second objection is that the author means that a multiplicity of possibilities in themselves cannot be conceived. The first objection is answered by distinguishing readiness from possibility as such. Readiness, considered merely as possibility, has no reality for the author. Those who say it exists mean that it exists as a readiness or feature of matter, which is the subject prepared to receive something. The author later distinguishes two kinds of possibility: possibility in itself, where an essence can be considered without contradiction as existing or not existing; and readiness for a particular way of existing, which arises only when the conditions are in place and obstacles removed. These differ in their subjects, as will be explained in the discussion of potentiality and actuality.

The author says elsewhere that readiness means removing an obstacle or its opposite, either fully (near potentiality) or partly (remote potentiality). Even if we grant that readiness has real existence because it is the very state of the prepared thing, it exists in relation to what it is prepared for, and as a weak existence of that thing. Prime matter itself exists only as a deep potential. The author’s descriptions of readiness as nothing, as a quality, or as a relation can be reconciled: it is “nothing” when viewed as potentiality in itself; a quality when viewed as a weak form of existence; and a relation when viewed as something that necessarily points to what the thing is ready to receive.

A further objection to the claim that possibility exists in the world is that it would make nonexistent essences real. Possibility in itself belongs to an essence considered just as it is. If it were a real feature, it would have to exist before the essence exists, even though it is not a substance. Also, if possibility were real, an endless chain would follow, since possibility itself would be possible. One cannot say that possibility is possible through itself: if it were a real possibility, it would be an essence under one of the ten categories, with existence added to it, and their relation would itself have to be qualified by possibility. Saying that possibility is possible through itself merely repeats the word; the question is how existence relates to it. — س ره

The reasoning is that if the possibilities were distinct in the world, our ability to recognize their differences would follow those real differences. But the argument being considered says that their differences come only from the mind. The claim that the possibilities exist in the world would therefore arise only because we assumed they were already different there. — س ره

This wording also allows for the case where each half gains a limited number of new possibilities. That case is covered by the later argument that the total would then be limited. Together, the possibilities can be grouped by whether they are unlimited or limited, and by whether they are already present or newly arise. The author’s five cases are: the same unlimited set in both halves; new unlimited sets; new limited sets; two already existing unlimited sets, each described as half the whole; or two limited sets already present. The source later addresses the fourth case. The argument resembles proofs used to show that a body’s active powers cannot be unlimited. — س ره

Someone might say that an unlimited set can still be smaller or larger than another unlimited set, as an unlimited series of tens is smaller than an unlimited series of hundreds. The first series is one tenth the size of the second, so each half could contain an unlimited set that is only half the total. — س ره

If these infinitely many parts cannot be divided, that is the view of al-Naẓẓām, who held that bodies are made of indivisible parts. If they can be divided, there would be an unlimited number of parts in fact, which would imply an unlimited size. A similar problem follows from some of the earlier possibilities, but the author gives a separate difficulty for each. — س ره

This objection seems to apply both to what is possible in itself and to something being ready for a change. The reply is that possibility, considered just as possibility, is an idea in the mind, even when the readiness for a change has some reality. The preparedness in an embryo to become human relates to the embryo; in this respect it is called readiness, and we say that the embryo is ready to become human. It also relates to the human being who may come to exist; in this respect it is called “possibility through preparation,” and we say that a human being can come to exist in the embryo. In this second sense it is only an idea. Also, even if readiness is real, whether considered as a state of the prepared thing or as a relation, a real feature need not have a real relation or a real thing at the other end of that relation. The author will discuss this later. — س ره
The Arabic word used here means a basin where water collects. It can also mean a plot of land someone takes for themselves or that a ruler assigns to them. Some copies instead read ijāda.
These are the two sides often called the side of light and the side of darkness, or the side turned toward God and the side turned toward the soul. — س ره

The claim “everything possible in itself is made of parts” and the claim “everything made of parts is possible in itself” each need their own proof. We cannot prove the second simply by turning the first sentence around; it is like separately proving that every immaterial being understands and that every being that understands is immaterial. — س ره

The difference from the earlier examples is that there the parts conflict with the composite: the parts are supposed to be necessary or impossible, while the whole is possible. In these two examples, the conflict is within the composite itself: it is impossible as a joining of contradictories, yet possible as a composite idea. The same applies to a composite of opposites, if we take each opposite together with the feature of being joined to the other. — س ره
This argument is answered by considering the First Effect. It is possible in itself, yet its nonexistence would entail the nonexistence of God, which is impossible. — س ره

The broad claim that follows—whether the consequence is necessarily existent—shows that the phrase “between a possible thing and something impossible” should be left out. This wording comes from the learned Dāmād’s The Clear Horizon: “The possibility of the antecedent belongs to it in itself, and it entails that the consequent is possible relative to the antecedent itself, not possible in itself. What follows from the link is only that the opposite of the consequent is not necessary relative to the antecedent, because the consequent is necessary relative to itself, whether it is necessarily present, necessarily absent, or neither when considered in itself.” This version is clearer. — س ره

That is, when one claim necessarily leads to another, the opposite of what follows cannot be necessary in relation to the first claim. This is a general possibility that can go with the consequent’s necessary existence, necessary nonexistence, or lack of necessity in either direction. This possibility too is relative to the antecedent, not to the consequent considered in itself. — س ره

The First Cause, considered in relation to the First Effect, is possible in the sense that it does not, by itself, require that the effect exist or not exist. The author sees this as close to a view expressed by al-Dawānī. — س ره

A further argument can be made. If causality is necessary, it is either identical with God’s essence or separate from it. Either way, the author’s conclusion follows, even without considering the impossibility of there being two necessary beings: if causality were separate, its effect could be absent while causality remained, unlike the First Cause, which is necessary. If causality is possible, it must itself have a cause, because possibility requires a cause and incidental features need an explanation. This leads either to an endless chain or to the same difficulty again. — س ره

The difficulty arises because something impossible through another must ultimately rest on something impossible in itself. Yet what is impossible through another is only possible in itself, so a possible thing appears to entail something impossible in itself. This would also destroy reasoning by contradiction, which infers that an assumption is impossible because it leads to an impossibility. The author’s answer is that the thing that entails the impossibility is not the possible essence itself, but its nonexistence. That nonexistence is not possible: it is necessary, while existence is impossible for it. The problem is therefore resolved, and reasoning by contradiction remains sound. — ط
“Necessity” here means absolute necessity in itself, timeless and unqualified.

This is also evidence that existence itself is what is real, including in the act of bringing things into existence. Those who say that essence is what is real still have to answer the argument. — س ره

One of the author’s contemporaries avoided saying that the First Effect’s existence is necessary through the necessity of God because he failed to distinguish three claims: necessary in itself; necessary because a Necessary Being exists; and necessary because that Being makes it so. He wrongly thought the second claim meant the effect was necessary in itself. The First Effect’s nonexistence is impossible because of the impossibility of God’s nonexistence, not because its own essence cannot be absent. Its existence is necessary through God’s necessity, not through itself and not because God separately imposes necessity on it. It remains through God, not through itself or a separate act of preserving it. This describes the world, where things are mostly equal in their own nature. God, by contrast, is necessary and lasting through Himself. — س ره
That is, someone might say this. — س ره

If “the thing” means the First Effect’s essence, it has no necessary link to the source. If it means its existence or nonexistence, its existence is necessary through the source and its nonexistence impossible through the source, so again no link has been shown. The reply is that “possible” means the essence, but the entailment does not come from the essence itself; it comes from the state of existence or nonexistence that belongs to it. More generally, overlooking the reality of essence causes many rules to be overlooked. Or “possibility” here may mean need and dependence. — س ره

The issue is that existence or nonexistence through another rests on a corresponding necessity or impossibility. Yet what is impossible through another is possible in itself, so a possible thing seems to entail something impossible in itself. That would undermine reasoning by contradiction, which uses the impossibility of a consequence to disprove its cause. The answer is that the thing entailing impossibility is not the possible thing itself, but its nonexistence. Nonexistence is not possible: it is impossible, while existence is impossible for it. The problem is resolved, and reasoning by contradiction remains sound. — س ره
